Let us begin where you already are. In the depth prerequisite node c6_chem_013, you learned that metals are lustrous, conductive and malleable. You probably remember holding a piece of copper wire, seeing its shine and knowing it carries electricity. You also learned that non-metals are the opposite in many ways: they are not shiny and do not conduct well. Now, in Class 7, we are not just repeating those facts; we are building a system around them. The direct prerequisite, c7_chem_001, gave you the big picture of how matter is classified by state and by composition. That picture is the frame in which we now place the idea of an element. If matter can be sorted into solid, liquid and gas, and also into pure substances and mixtures, then an element is a pure substance made of only one kind of atom. Once you see that, classifying elements as metals, non-metals or metalloids becomes a natural next step.

Think of the metal group first. Imagine a bright copper pot from a market in Moradabad, the brass- and copper-working city of Uttar Pradesh. Its shine is what we call lustrous. Press a thin sheet of gold between your fingers; it flattens without cracking because it is malleable. Connect a bulb with copper wire, and it glows because copper is conductive. These three properties together are the signature of a typical metal. But now look more closely. Is every hard, shiny thing a metal? Not at all. A diamond is hard and can sparkle, yet it is a form of carbon, a non-metal. So a good answer does not say "shiny means metal"; it says "metals are usually lustrous, and this is one clue, but we confirm the identity by checking conductivity and malleability as well." A weak answer simply lists examples without explaining the pattern; a strong answer uses the pattern to explain the examples.

Next, consider the non-metals. Picture a small heap of yellow sulphur powder in a laboratory in Kolkata. It is dull, not bright, and if you press it, it crumbles rather than spreads. Oxygen is invisible, but it supports burning. Carbon, in the form of graphite, can actually conduct electricity, which surprises many students and shows that exceptions matter. When you describe non-metals, do not just say "they are not metals." Say "they are generally dull, poor conductors and brittle, and they form acidic or neutral oxides when they react with oxygen." This is the deeper classification that c7_chem_006 wants you to reach.

Now for the metalloids, the bridge group. Silicon, mined and refined in regions such as Karnataka and Tamil Nadu for the electronics industry, is neither clearly a metal nor clearly a non-metal. It has a metallic appearance but its conductivity is much lower than that of copper or silver and can be tuned by adding tiny amounts of other substances. This is why your phone and laptop chips are made from silicon. A good answer explains that a metalloid is like a person with dual citizenship: it shares some rights and duties with both neighbours, but does not fully belong to either.

Let us also look at mixtures and separation. You have already learned that a mixture keeps the properties of its components, while a compound has a fixed composition and new properties. In this node, the emphasis is on the principle behind separation. Ask yourself, what makes the parts different from one another? If one part is magnetic and the other is not, use a magnet. If one dissolves and the other does not, dissolve and filter. If one has a lower boiling point, distil. If the colours are different and move at different rates through filter paper, use chromatography. Each method is a clever use of a physical difference. When you write an exam answer, do not merely name the method. Name the method and explain the difference it uses.

What does the board examiner expect? The examiner wants you to classify correctly, to use the right vocabulary such as lustrous, conductive, malleable, reactivity, metalloid and separation, and to give a reason for every choice. Examiners have noticed that students often confuse physical appearance with chemical identity, or that they state facts without conditions. So always answer with "because" and "therefore." For example: "Sulphur is a non-metal because it is dull and does not conduct electricity." Practice writing in full sentences, not half-finished lists, and you will meet the board standard.

Mixtures are like a bowl of mixed nuts; we can separate them using small differences, such as size or stickiness.

Misconception 1 -- "If a substance looks shiny, it must be a metal." Many students, echoing the kind of confusion examiners noted when candidates chose Nickel or were unsure about Hydrogen, think that appearance alone decides the group. Correction: Lustre is only one clue. We must also test conductivity, malleability and, most importantly, the chemical properties such as the kind of oxide formed. Diamond is shiny but is a non-metal; graphite is dull-looking yet conducts electricity. A good classification combines several tests.

Misconception 2 -- "A compound that contains a metal and a non-metal is always ionic, so carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) should be ionic." Examiners have reported that some candidates chose NaCl and assumed any formula with a familiar non-metal was ionic, revealing a confusion between elements and compounds. Correction: The metal/non-metal classification applies to elements, not automatically to every compound. CCl4 is a covalent compound made of two non-metals, carbon and chlorine. When elements combine, the bonding depends on the types of atoms involved, not just on the presence of a non-metal.

Misconception 3 -- "All metals are equally reactive, and strong metals do not react." Some students think that because iron is strong and used in bridges, it must be unreactive, or they mix up the words reactivity and hardness. Correction: Reactivity and physical strength are different. Gold is unreactive and does not tarnish, but iron reacts with oxygen and water to form rust. Copper reacts slowly to form green patina. So we cannot judge reactivity from how hard or heavy a metal is; we must look at how it behaves with air, water and acids.

Q1 (recall): Define the terms element, metal, non-metal and metalloid, and give one example of each. List the main physical properties used to decide whether an element is a metal or a non-metal.
Answer: An element is a pure substance that is made of only one kind of atom and cannot be broken down into anything simpler by ordinary chemical means. Examples include iron, copper, sulphur, oxygen and silicon. A metal is an element that is generally hard, lustrous, malleable, ductile and a good conductor of heat and electricity; for example, copper is used in electrical wires because it is highly conductive, and gold is used in ornaments because it is lustrous and can be drawn into thin wires. A non-metal is an element that usually lacks metallic shine, is not malleable, is often brittle if solid, and is a poor conductor of heat and electricity; sulphur is a dull, yellow solid that breaks easily, while oxygen is a colourless gas that supports burning and respiration. A metalloid is an element that has properties intermediate between those of metals and non-metals; the best-known example is silicon, which looks like a metal but does not conduct electricity as well as copper, and its conductivity can be controlled for use in electronic chips. The main physical properties used to classify an element are lustre, conductivity, malleability and ductility, along with the way the element feels when struck or pressed.

Q2 (reasoning): Why is copper used for electrical wiring, while sulphur is not used for this purpose? Explain by comparing the two elements in terms of their classification and properties.
Answer: Copper is chosen for electrical wiring because it is a metal, and metals are good conductors of electricity. Copper in particular has a bright lustrous surface, is highly malleable, and can be drawn into long, thin wires without breaking. These properties come from the way the atoms in a metal are arranged in a lattice with free-moving electrons that carry electric current. Sulphur, on the other hand, is a non-metal. It is dull, brittle and does not allow electricity to pass through it; in fact, solid sulphur is an electrical insulator. If you tried to make a wire from sulphur, it would crack and crumble, and it would not carry any current. Therefore, copper is suitable for wiring because of its metallic properties of conductivity and malleability, whereas sulphur fails on both counts because of its non-metallic properties. This comparison shows that the classification of an element as a metal or a non-metal is directly linked to its uses in everyday life.

Q3 (evaluate): A student says, "All the components of any mixture can be separated by filtration." Evaluate this statement, giving a balanced argument with at least one example in favour and one against, and state the correct principle for separating mixtures.
Answer: The statement is not fully correct, so it should be evaluated carefully. Filtration is a useful separation technique, but it only works when there is a clear difference in particle size or in the state of the components, specifically when a solid is mixed with a liquid or a gas and the solid particles are large enough to be trapped by the filter paper. For example, a mixture of sand and water can be separated by filtration because sand is an insoluble solid that does not pass through the pores of the filter. Similarly, a mixture of chalk and water can be separated in this way.

However, many mixtures cannot be separated by filtration. If the solid is very fine and passes through the filter, or if the mixture is of two dissolved solids in water, filtration will fail. For instance, common salt dissolved in seawater or in water from the salt pans of Gujarat cannot be separated by filtration because the salt particles are too small and have dissolved. Instead, evaporation is used because the water turns to vapour and leaves the salt behind. A mixture of alcohol and water cannot be separated by filtration either, because both are liquids; distillation is the right method because it uses the difference in boiling points. A mixture of iron filings and sulphur can be separated with a magnet because iron is magnetic, a property that has nothing to do with particle size. The correct principle for separating mixtures is that every method must use a physical difference between the components, whether that difference is solubility, magnetism, boiling point, size or the speed at which substances move through a medium. Therefore, while filtration is a valuable technique, it is not universal, and the choice of method must depend on the actual properties of the mixture in question.

Q4 (apply): You are given a mixture of iron filings, sulphur powder and common salt. Describe a step-by-step method, with reasons, to obtain each component separately in its pure form.
Answer: First, use a magnet to remove the iron filings from the mixture. Iron is magnetic, while sulphur and common salt are not, so the iron filings will stick to the magnet and can be collected. This takes advantage of the difference in magnetic property between the components. Next, add the remaining mixture to water and stir well. Common salt is soluble in water, but sulphur is not, so the salt dissolves while the sulphur remains as an insoluble solid. Filter the mixture using filter paper. The insoluble sulphur will be left on the filter paper as the residue; it can be washed with a little distilled water and dried. The filtrate will be a solution of salt in water. Finally, pour the filtrate into an evaporating dish and heat it gently over a water bath or low flame. The water will evaporate, and the white crystals of common salt will be left behind. By choosing three different physical properties, magnetism, solubility in water and the volatility of water, we have separated all three components cleanly. This is a practical illustration of the principle that the components of a mixture keep their individual properties, so we can use these properties to separate them.

Q5 (create): Design a simple board game for Class 6 students to learn the difference between metals, non-metals and metalloids. Name the game, list the rules, and explain how playing it will help students remember the properties of these elements.
Answer: The game can be called "Element Quest: Metal, Non-Metal or Metalloid?" It is a board game for two to four players, played on a winding path across a large sheet. Each space on the path has a coloured square: silver for metal, yellow for non-metal and purple for metalloid. Each player rolls a die and moves the number of spaces. When a player lands on a square, he or she picks a card from the matching pile. The card describes an element, such as "This element is used in electrical wires and is very malleable" or "This element is the main ingredient in sand and computer chips." The player must say whether the element is a metal, a non-metal or a metalloid and give one reason. If the answer is correct, the player moves two extra spaces; if it is wrong, the player must read the correction card and stay where he or she is.

The game includes "Challenge" spaces where players must match properties with examples, such as pairing "lustrous" with "gold," "brittle" with "sulphur," or "used in electronics" with "silicon." There is also a "Mix-Up" space where the player must suggest one method for separating a given mixture and explain the principle. The winner is the first player to reach the final square, called the "Periodic Castle." Playing this game will help students remember that classification is based on a pattern of properties, not on random facts. The repeated act of explaining "because" reinforces the links between appearance, conductivity, malleability, reactivity and real-world uses, making the concepts stick better than simple memorisation.

title: Reactivity series of metals
definition:
The reactivity series of metals is a ranked list of common metals arranged in order of their chemical reactivity, from the most reactive to the least reactive. The standard order you must remember for the ICSE Class 8 syllabus is: potassium > sodium > calcium > magnesium > aluminium > zinc > iron > copper > silver > gold. This order is built on how vigorously a metal reacts with cold water, hot water, steam and dilute acids, and on whether one metal can displace another metal from its compound. At the top, potassium and sodium are so reactive that they fizz, dart about and may even catch fire when dropped into cold water, so they are stored under oil. Calcium reacts with cold water more gently, producing hydrogen gas and a milky suspension of calcium hydroxide. Magnesium reacts only slowly with cold water but burns brightly in steam to form magnesium oxide and hydrogen. Aluminium, zinc and iron react with steam when heated, giving their oxides and hydrogen, but they do not react usefully with cold water. Copper, silver and gold are far less reactive and do not react with water or dilute acids under ordinary conditions; that is why gold and silver can occur in nature as free metals, for example in the Kolar Gold Fields of Karnataka or in the silver-rich ores of Rajasthan.

Reactivity is best understood as a metal's eagerness to lose electrons and become a positive ion, called a cation. The higher a metal sits in the series, the more readily it loses electrons. This idea explains the most important use of the reactivity series: predicting displacement reactions. A more reactive metal will displace a less reactive metal from an aqueous solution of its salt, because the more reactive metal has a stronger tendency to form ions in solution. For instance, when a strip of zinc is dipped into blue copper(II) sulphate solution, the zinc slowly disappears and a reddish-brown coating of copper appears; the blue colour fades because zinc has displaced copper from the solution, forming colourless zinc sulphate. Similarly, when an iron nail is placed in copper(II) sulphate solution, the iron becomes coated with copper and the solution loses its blue colour. The reverse does not happen: a copper strip placed in zinc sulphate or iron(II) sulphate solution will show no reaction, because copper is less reactive than both zinc and iron.

The reactivity series also helps us explain why some metals are extracted from their ores by simple heating, while others need smelting or electrolysis. Reactive metals such as aluminium need expensive extraction because they hold their oxygen very tightly, whereas less reactive metals such as iron can be extracted from haematite in the blast furnaces of Rourkela or Durgapur using coke as a reducing agent. Copper from the Khetri mines of Rajasthan and iron from the Singhbhum belt of Jharkhand make sense in an Indian context once you see that India's mineral wealth and the reactivity of the metal together decide how the metal is obtained. The key terms to carry forward are reactivity series, reactive metal, less reactive metal, displacement, and the names of the metals themselves: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper, silver and gold.

Copper, silver and gold sit near the bottom of the ladder; they remain quiet even in steam or dilute acids and are sometimes found almost pure in nature.

The reactivity series is not just a list to memorise. It is a prediction tool. When you are asked whether one metal will displace another, compare their positions. A more reactive metal will displace a less reactive metal from its compound. For example, zinc is above copper, so a zinc granule placed in blue copper(II) sulphate solution will lose its silvery shine, copper metal will deposit as a reddish solid, and the blue colour will fade. A good answer names both metals, states the order and describes the observation. A weak answer only writes "displacement happens" or "zinc reacts," which is too vague for the board exam. If you had placed a copper strip in zinc sulphate, nothing would have happened, and you must be able to explain why: copper is below zinc, so it cannot displace zinc.

Let us also be careful about the language of the exam. board examiners often note that students lose marks by giving incomplete answers. In the 2024 Common board exam error pattern, examiners pointed out that some candidates wrote only the word "concentrated" instead of the full "concentrated sulphuric acid" and so lost credit. Always give the full order or the complete sentence, such as "Zinc is more reactive than copper, so zinc displaces copper from copper(II) sulphate solution." In the Common board exam error pattern, candidates also confused electrochemical series with reactivity series while identifying anode and cathode. Keep the two ideas separate: the reactivity series tells you about displacement, while electrochemical series is for cells and electrode signs.

For the ICSE board, expect questions that ask you to arrange the ten common metals, to explain why a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one, and to predict whether a given displacement reaction will occur. Examiners want accurate, complete statements and clear reasoning, not half-remembered fragments.

When an iron nail is placed in copper(II) sulphate solution, each iron atom gives up two electrons to become an iron(II) ion and enters the solution. The copper(II) ions in the solution accept these electrons and are reduced to copper atoms, which settle as a reddish-brown solid on the nail. The blue colour of the copper(II) sulphate solution fades because the copper ions are being removed and replaced by colourless iron(II) ions. The overall reaction is Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu. This is a single displacement reaction driven by the difference in reactivity. Copper cannot do the same to iron because copper atoms hold their electrons more tightly and are less willing to become ions.

Q3 (evaluate): A student claims that, if copper powder is heated strongly in zinc sulphate solution for a long time, copper will finally displace zinc from the solution because heat gives the copper atoms enough energy. Evaluate this statement, giving a balanced argument.
Answer: The student's claim is not correct for ordinary laboratory conditions, and the reasoning confuses the effect of heat on reaction speed with the possibility of the reaction itself. The reactivity series is based on the inherent tendency of metals to lose electrons. Zinc is above copper, so zinc atoms have a stronger tendency to form ions than copper atoms do. This means zinc can displace copper from copper(II) sulphate, but copper cannot displace zinc from zinc sulphate. Heating the mixture may make the particles move faster and could speed up a reaction that is already possible, but it cannot reverse the order of reactivity. No amount of ordinary heating will make copper atoms give away electrons to zinc ions because copper is the less reactive metal. On the other hand, the balanced part of the argument is that energy from an external electric current, as in electrolysis, can force a non-spontaneous change. In electrolysis, electrical energy drives oxidation and reduction in a way that heat alone cannot. However, in the context of a simple displacement reaction, the correct evaluation is that copper will not displace zinc from zinc sulphate, even on strong heating, because copper is below zinc in the reactivity series.

Q4 (apply): Predict whether the following displacement reactions will occur. Where a reaction occurs, write the balanced word or chemical equation; where it does not, write "no reaction" and give a reason. (i) Zinc granules are added to copper(II) sulphate solution. (ii) A copper wire is dipped into iron(II) sulphate solution. (iii) A magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid.
Answer: (i) The reaction will occur because zinc is above copper in the reactivity series. Zinc is more reactive and displaces copper from copper(II) sulphate. The blue solution slowly becomes colourless as zinc sulphate forms, and reddish-brown copper metal is deposited. The equation is Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu. (ii) No reaction will occur. Copper is below iron in the reactivity series, so copper cannot displace iron from iron(II) sulphate solution. The copper wire remains unchanged and the green colour of iron(II) sulphate stays the same. (iii) The reaction will occur because magnesium is well above hydrogen in the reactivity series. Magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to form magnesium chloride and hydrogen gas, which is seen as brisk effervescence. The equation is Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2. These three examples show how the reactivity series can be used to predict not only metal-to-metal displacement but also reaction with acids.

Q5 (create): Design a simple laboratory experiment, using zinc granules, an iron nail and a piece of copper wire, to show the relative reactivity of these three metals. Include the materials, procedure, observation table and the expected conclusion.
Answer: The experiment can be performed with three small test tubes, copper(II) sulphate solution, iron(II) sulphate solution, zinc sulphate solution, zinc granules, a clean iron nail and a small piece of copper wire. Label three test tubes A, B and C. In tube A place zinc granules in copper(II) sulphate solution. In tube B place the iron nail in copper(II) sulphate solution. In tube C place the copper wire in zinc sulphate solution. For an extra comparison, you may also place zinc in iron(II) sulphate. Leave the tubes for about fifteen minutes and observe. In tube A, the zinc granules become coated with a reddish-brown solid and the blue colour fades, showing zinc displaces copper. In tube B, the iron nail also becomes coated with copper and the blue colour fades, but more slowly, showing iron is less reactive than zinc. In tube C, no change is seen, confirming copper cannot displace zinc. The conclusion is that the reactivity order among these three metals is zinc > iron > copper. For safety, wear gloves and goggles; do not touch the metals with bare hands after the reaction; and wash the apparatus thoroughly after use.
